title: Finals Exam Reviewer
description: Web Services and SOAP, REST and Consuming APIs, and Reliable and Secure Data Exchange (serialization, access control, data protection). Multiple choice, from remembering to scenario and evaluating items.

questions.question: A software component that lets two applications communicate and exchange data over a network.
Web services communicate using open, agreed standards of the web, such as:
Two applications built on different platforms can still talk through a web service because:
options: Both share one database and one server
Both are rewritten in one common language
Both can read each other's source code
Both follow the same published contract
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 - Web Services and SOAP. Neither side needs to know how the other was built internally.

questions.question: Systems interact through a published contract, not each other's internal code, so one can change without breaking the other.
One service can be consumed by many applications: web, mobile, and other back-end systems.
Open standards (HTTP, XML, JSON) let products from different vendors work together.
A strict protocol using XML and a WSDL contract, common in enterprise and high-security systems.
An architectural style using plain HTTP, usually with JSON; lightweight and common for web and mobile.
Older, simple styles for calling a remote method and passing parameters, rarely used in new systems.
The three interactions of a service-oriented architecture are:
In the web service architecture, which role hosts the service and publishes its WSDL?
In the web service architecture, which role searches the directory and retrieves the WSDL?
In the web service architecture, the UDDI directory plays the role of the:
In the bind and invoke step, the requester:
options: Registers its WSDL file in the directory
Searches the registry directory for a matching service
Groups services by category for browsing
Uses the WSDL to call the service at its endpoint

questions.question: A design approach where software is built as a set of reusable, independent services.
What is the most common way to put SOA into practice?
SOA principle: small services can be combined into larger business processes.
SOA principle: services can be published and found through a registry.
SOA principle: each service exposes a clear, agreed interface.
SOAP carries the message, WSDL ______, and UDDI ______.
options: describes the service; helps clients find it
encrypts the message; routes the message
helps clients find it; describes the service
stores the data; validates the schema

questions.question: Which core building block is the service contract?
Which core building block is the directory where services are published so clients can discover them?
XML stands for:
Which statement about the basic rules of XML is correct?
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 - Web Services and SOAP. Well formed, case sensitive, exactly one root element.

questions.question: Why is this XML not a valid document?
options: It has more than one root element
Its tags do not follow case sensitivity
It is missing a SOAP Header
Its values are not in quotes
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 - Web Services and SOAP. There must be exactly one root element.

questions.question: SOAP messages are written entirely in:
SOAP stands for:
SOAP is transport independent but is most commonly sent over:
Why do both sides always know exactly how to read a SOAP message?
options: The server sends its source code first
The client and server share one database
The message is converted to plain text
The format is strict and well defined

questions.question: The root element that marks the start and end of a SOAP message.
The optional part of a SOAP message that carries metadata such as authentication, transaction, and routing information.
The required part of a SOAP message that carries the actual request or response data.
In this SOAP message, what does the Header carry?
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 - Web Services and SOAP. The Header is optional; here it carries the auth token.

questions.question: In this SOAP message, what is the Body asking for?
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 - Web Services and SOAP. A response looks the same, with the result inside the Body.

questions.question: When something goes wrong, the server returns a SOAP Fault. Where is it placed?
In this SOAP Fault, which element gives the human readable explanation of the error?
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 - Web Services and SOAP. faultcode identifies the type of error.

questions.question: Which SOAP Fault element is optional and names who caused the fault?
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 - Web Services and SOAP. detail holds application-specific error details.

questions.question: In the SOAP message flow, what does the server send back when the request fails?
options: An empty Envelope with no Body
A UDDI entry pointing to another service
A SOAP Fault instead of a normal result
A new WSDL describing the error

questions.question: A SOAP message that looks like a remote method call, carrying an operation name and its parameters, uses which style?
Which SOAP messaging style carries a full XML document, is more loosely coupled, and is easier to validate against a schema?
Why do most modern SOAP services use the document style with literal encoding?
options: Matching a method signature is faster and easier to validate
It lets SOAP messages be written in JSON
It removes the need for a WSDL contract
Validating a whole document against a schema is more reliable

questions.question: WSDL stands for:
Which WSDL element lists the operations the service offers?
Which WSDL element states the protocol and format used?
Which WSDL element gives the endpoint address (URL)?
Why can a developer generate working client code from a WSDL alone?
options: The WSDL describes every operation, message, data type, and endpoint
The WSDL contains the provider's full source code and database
The SOAP Header carries the generated code to the client
The UDDI registry sends ready-made classes to every client

questions.question: Tools such as wsimport (Java) and svcutil (.NET) build client code from:
UDDI stands for:
In UDDI, which part holds technical details on how to connect to and call the service?
In UDDI, which part groups services by category so clients can browse by type?
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 - Web Services and SOAP. White pages hold the business name and contact information.

questions.question: Why is UDDI less common today?
options: SOAP messages can no longer be sent over HTTP connections
REST replaced XML in every SOAP service
Many services are shared directly through their WSDL

questions.question: Which WS-* standard adds authentication, encryption, and message integrity?
Which WS-* standard puts routing and addressing information inside the message?
Which WS-* standard guarantees delivery even if the network fails temporarily?
Which WS-* standard coordinates a transaction across several services?
How does WS-Security differ from relying only on HTTPS?
options: It lets the SOAP message be sent without using any XML
It protects the message itself, not just the connection
It makes the XML message smaller and faster to send over HTTP
It removes the need for a WSDL contract between the parties

questions.question: A dedicated tool to test, inspect, and debug SOAP services.
Which is a trade-off (limitation) of SOAP?
options: Strong typing through a WSDL contract

questions.question: Which is a strength of SOAP?
options: It is faster than lightweight styles
Messages are small, light, and quick to send
Setup is simple and very flexible
Built-in standards for security and reliability

questions.question: Which situation is the best fit for SOAP?
options: An interbank payment needing formal security and reliability
A web page loading a short list of products
A quick weather widget for a personal blog site
A public mobile API that must stay light, simple, and fast
questions.explanation: Lesson 1 - Web Services and SOAP. When to use SOAP: banking, payments, telecom; strict contracts; guaranteed messaging.

questions.question: What is a SOAP Fault?
options: A WSDL element that describes the endpoint address of the service
An element in the Body that reports an error instead of a normal result
The root element that marks the start and end of a SOAP message
An optional element in the Header that carries authentication data

questions.question: What is SOAP?
options: An architectural style that treats data as resources over HTTP
A registry where providers publish services for clients to find
A strict XML-based protocol for exchanging structured information
A lightweight text format built from key and value pairs

questions.question: API stands for:
A defined set of rules that lets one program request data or services from another.
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 - REST and Consuming APIs. A web API exposes those rules over the web, usually through HTTP.

questions.question: In the restaurant analogy, what represents the API?
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 - REST and Consuming APIs. The diner orders without seeing the kitchen.

questions.question: In the restaurant analogy, what does the API hide from the diner (client)?
options: The waiter carrying the order to the kitchen
The menu of things to order
The kitchen, where the work is done

questions.question: API style with one endpoint where the client asks for exactly the data it needs, reducing over-fetching.
High-performance API style using a binary format over HTTP/2, common between back-end services.
REST stands for:
REST is best described as:
options: A strict protocol with a fixed XML format
A binary format that runs over HTTP/2
An architectural style, a set of guidelines
A registry where services are published

questions.question: An API that follows the REST guidelines is described as:
REST principle: each request carries all the information it needs, and the server keeps no session between calls.
REST principle: a client cannot tell whether it talks to the server directly or through an intermediary.
REST principle: responses can be stored and reused to reduce load and improve performance.
REST principle: resources are accessed in one consistent, predictable way.
REST principle: the client and the server are separate, and each can change without affecting the other.
Each resource in REST is identified by a unique:
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 - REST and Consuming APIs. A resource is any object or piece of data: a user, a product, an order.

questions.question: Which URI refers to the grades of student 42?
Which endpoint follows the REST naming best practice?
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 - REST and Consuming APIs. Use nouns in the URL; the HTTP method decides the action.

questions.question: JSON stands for:
In JSON, objects use ____ and arrays use ____.
Which is NOT one of the JSON value types?
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 - REST and Consuming APIs. Values: string, number, boolean, null, object, or array.

questions.question: In this response, what type of value is stored in "active"?
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 - REST and Consuming APIs. true without quotes is a boolean.
questions.code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "id": 42,
  "name": "Juan dela Cruz",
  "course": "BSIT",
  "active": true
}

questions.question: Why do REST APIs usually exchange data as JSON?
options: It encrypts the data it carries
It is lightweight and easy to read
It has a strict schema like a WSDL
It is the only format HTTP accepts

questions.question: Which HTTP method maps to the Create operation?
Which HTTP method modifies only part of a resource?
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 - REST and Consuming APIs. PUT replaces the whole resource.

questions.question: What does PUT /students/42 do?
A method is called safe when:
options: It always returns a 200 OK status code
Calling it many times has the same effect
It only reads data and never changes it
It sends its data through HTTPS only

questions.question: A method is idempotent when:
options: It needs a valid token in the Authorization header to run
Calling it once or many times has the same final effect
It only reads data and never changes it
It always creates a brand new resource

questions.question: Which HTTP method is both safe and idempotent?
Which HTTP method is neither safe nor idempotent?
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 - REST and Consuming APIs. Each POST creates a new resource.

questions.question: Why is DELETE idempotent even though it changes data?
options: It never changes any data on the server
It can only be sent once per session
The server caches the deleted resource
The resource is gone after the first call

questions.question: Why can sending the same POST request twice create two resources?
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 - REST and Consuming APIs. Each POST call creates a new resource.

questions.question: Which status code family means the problem is in the request itself?
A 5xx status code means:
options: The request was received and processed
The server failed to handle a valid request
The request itself was badly formed
Further action is needed to complete the request

questions.question: Which status code means a new resource was created?
Which status code belongs to the 3xx Redirection family?
A request returns 404. What does it tell the developer?
options: The token expired and the user must sign in again
The server crashed on a valid request
The endpoint path or resource is not found

questions.question: In this request, which part is the query string (filters or options)?
In this request, which part is the base URL (where the API lives)?
A request body (usually JSON) is sent with which methods?
Which request header states the format the client wants, such as application/json?
Which request header carries credentials, such as a token?
Which response header tells how the response may be cached?
In content negotiation, the client asks with ______ and the server replies with a matching ______.
In this response, what does the Content-Type header tell the client?
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 - REST and Consuming APIs. The status line 200 OK means success; the header says the body is JSON.
questions.code:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json

{
  "id": 42,
  "name": "Juan dela Cruz",
  "course": "BSIT",
  "active": true
}

questions.question: What does /students?page=2&limit=20 return?
options: The second page of results, 20 per page
The first 2 students, sorted by limit

questions.question: Which query parameter sorts the results?
What is pagination in a REST API?
options: Splitting one resource into two separate endpoints with new names
Ordering the results of a collection by one field, e.g., ?sort=name
Returning a large collection in smaller pages, e.g., ?page=2&limit=20
Returning only the records that match a value, e.g., ?course=BSIT

questions.question: Why must every REST request prove who is calling?
options: REST messages are written in XML
REST has no status codes for reporting errors
REST uses the WSDL as its contract
REST is stateless, so no session is kept

questions.question: A signed token sent in the Authorization header, common for logged-in users.
What is OAuth 2.0?
options: A standard flow that grants limited access without a password
A browser rule on which websites may call your API
A simple secret string sent in a header or a query string
A signed token that the server verifies on each request

questions.question: What must be used with every authentication method so credentials are encrypted in transit?
Unlike a SOAP Fault, how does REST report an error?
options: With a faultcode inside the SOAP Envelope
With an HTTP status code plus a JSON body
With a 200 OK and an empty body
With a new WSDL describing the error

questions.question: What does this response tell the client?
Which is a REST error-handling rule from the lesson?
options: Put the error inside a SOAP Fault
Always send 500 for every kind of error
Return errors as plain HTML pages
Never send 200 OK for a failed request

questions.question: Why should an API be versioned, e.g., /v1/students?
options: So the API can return 200 OK for every error
So each request can skip the Authorization header
So the server can keep a session for each client
So changes do not break existing clients

questions.question: Which is a REST API design best practice?
options: Keep naming, casing, and response shapes uniform
Return 200 OK even when a request fails
Store a session for each client on the server
Put verbs such as get in every endpoint
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 - REST and Consuming APIs. Be consistent.

questions.question: What is the first step in consuming a REST API?
questions.explanation: Lesson 2 - REST and Consuming APIs. The API contract is the documentation.

questions.question: Which reminder applies when consuming an API?
options: Skip the status code and read the body directly
Never hard-code secrets in client-side code
Send data in any format you prefer

questions.question: A tool for sending requests straight from the command line, useful for quick checks.
A tool to document an API and let others try its endpoints interactively.
Which comparison of SOAP and REST is correct?
options: Both are strict protocols that use only XML
Both are styles that use only JSON over HTTP
SOAP is a protocol; REST is an architectural style
SOAP is an architectural style; REST is a protocol

questions.question: Which comparison of transport is correct?
options: SOAP: HTTP only; REST: HTTP, SMTP, and more
Both SOAP and REST use HTTP only
Both SOAP and REST use SMTP only
SOAP: HTTP, SMTP, and more; REST: HTTP only

questions.question: Which comparison of contracts is correct?
options: SOAP: WSDL (strict); REST: optional, e.g., OpenAPI
Neither one can have any contract
SOAP: optional, e.g., OpenAPI; REST: WSDL (strict)
Both require a strict WSDL contract

questions.question: REST is usually the better choice for:
options: Systems that require a strict WSDL contract
Messages that must use only the XML format

questions.question: What is a query string in a REST request?
options: The part that tells where the API lives, e.g., https://api.school.edu
The part after ? that adds filters or options, e.g., ?active=true
The part that identifies the resource, e.g., /students/42
The part that names the action to perform, e.g., GET

questions.question: What is content negotiation?
options: The server keeps a session so the client does not resend its token each time
The client and server agree on a price for using the API before the first request
The client asks for a format with Accept and the server replies with a matching Content-Type
The client sends its credentials in the query string instead of a header

questions.question: What is a resource in REST?
options: A method that decides the action, such as GET or POST
Any object or piece of data, such as a user, product, or order
A status code that reports the result of a request
A header that carries credentials, such as a token

questions.question: The three layers of reliable and secure data exchange, in order:
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: What does "reliable is not the same as safe" mean?
options: Security can be added at the end
You need all three layers together
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Converting an in-memory object into portable text or bytes so it can travel over a network or be saved to disk.
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Parsing text or bytes back into a usable object on the other side.
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Serialization and deserialization are also called:
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Turning the raw string "juan" into structured code name: "juan" is called:
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange. Serializing goes the other way: structured code into a raw string.

questions.question: The round-trip rule says deserialize(serialize(x)) must:
options: Turn x into a JSON string every time
Return x as a smaller binary format
Encrypt x before it reaches the client over the network
Give back x with the same values and structure
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange. If not, your data exchange has a bug.

questions.question: In this code, what does JSON.stringify(order) do?
options: Turns the object into JSON text
Turns JSON text into an object
Checks the JSON against a schema
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: In this code, what does res.json(order) do?
options: Turns JSON text into an object
Saves the JSON text to the disk
Sends JSON and sets the Content-Type
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Why should JSON.parse always be wrapped in try/catch?
options: So the JSON is encrypted in transit
So the keys become double quoted
So bad input cannot crash the server
So the parse runs faster on the server
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Which statement about JSON is correct?
options: Comments are allowed inside the data
Keys are always strings in double quotes
Keys may be numbers without quotes
It has ten value types, including date
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Which format is the default for web and mobile APIs?
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Which format is verbose but strict and self-describing, still common in SOAP, banking, and government systems?
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Which format is the most readable and is used for configuration files (Docker, Kubernetes, CI)?
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Protocol Buffers and MessagePack are examples of which kind of format?
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange. Compact, fast, and schema-driven, for heavy internal service-to-service traffic.

questions.question: Which question does Authentication (AuthN) answer?
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange. Authentication always comes first.

questions.question: Which question does Authorization (AuthZ) answer?
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Which status code means "we do not know who you are" (authentication failed)?
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Which status code means "we know you, but you are not allowed" (authorization failed)?
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: What does HTTPS / TLS do?
options: Limits the number of requests per window for each client
Turns objects into portable JSON text
Groups permissions into roles for users
Encrypts traffic in transit and confirms the real server
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange. Mandatory for every production API.

questions.question: Which is true about an API key?
options: Good for service-to-service, weak at proving a user
Encrypted, so it is safe to commit to code
Only works over plain HTTP, never HTTPS
Best way to prove a specific logged-in user in every app
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Why should secrets never be put in a JWT payload?
options: It is deleted after the first request
It is signed, not encrypted, so anyone can read it
It is encrypted, so the server cannot read it
It is stored in the server's database
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Which part of a JWT names the algorithm that signs the token?
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange. Payload: user id, role, expiry (readable). Signature: proves it was not altered.

questions.question: Which part of a JWT proves the token was not altered and is made with a secret key?
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Why is JWT called stateless?
options: The server verifies the signature with no database lookup
The server keeps a session for each token
The token is encrypted so no one but the server can read it
The token never expires once it is issued
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Which OAuth 2.0 flow is used for service-to-service access?
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange. Authorization-code flow is for humans (Login with Google).

questions.question: What is RBAC (role-based access control)?
options: Encrypting stored data so that only the owner can read it
Grouping permissions into roles and giving each role only what it needs
Limiting the number of requests a client can send per window
Signing a token so the server can verify it with no lookup
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: In RBAC, where should permissions be enforced?
options: In the client app's local storage
On the server, never trust the client
In the JWT payload, kept as a secret
In the browser, through hidden buttons
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: The CIA triad stands for:
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Which technique serves Confidentiality?
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Symmetric encryption:
options: Cannot be used for bulk data at all
Is slower and used only for key exchange
Uses a public key and a private key
Uses one shared key to encrypt and decrypt
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange. Example: AES. Challenge: sharing the key safely.

questions.question: Asymmetric encryption:
options: One shared key encrypts and decrypts
Faster than symmetric for bulk data
Public key encrypts, private key decrypts
Turns data into a one-way fingerprint
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange. Example: RSA, ECC. TLS combines both.

questions.question: If data is encrypted in transit (TLS) but stored as plain text, what is still exposed?
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange. Protect data in transit AND at rest.

questions.question: How should passwords be stored?
options: Hashed with MD5 or SHA-1 for speed
Encrypted so they can be decrypted and read back later
Saved as plain text in a safe table
Hashed with a slow salted algorithm like bcrypt
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: A one-way fingerprint: the same input always gives the same result, but it cannot be reversed.
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: What is HMAC?
options: A list of trusted origins that are allowed to call the API from a browser
A role that groups permissions so each user gets only what is needed
A public key that encrypts a message so only the private key can decrypt it
A hash of the message plus a shared secret, used to confirm it is authentic and unchanged
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: Private key signs, public key verifies, so the signer cannot later deny it. This property is called:
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange. Digital signatures are best across organizations.

questions.question: Rebuilding untrusted input into objects without checks is called:
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange. A crafted payload can overwrite fields or run code. A classic OWASP Top 10 risk.

questions.question: Which is the defense against insecure deserialization?
options: Validate against a schema and prefer JSON
Trust fields that came from the client
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: When validating input, you should:
options: Use an allowlist and validate at the boundary
Trust input that is already in JSON
Use a blocklist after the business logic
Validate only after saving the data
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: What is rate limiting?
options: Encrypting traffic between the client and server
Checking input against an allowlist at the boundary
Capping requests per time window (429 Too Many Requests)
Allowing only trusted websites to call the API
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange. Stops brute force and scraping and protects availability.

questions.question: Which rule about CORS is correct?
options: Use CORS on the server to hash the passwords
Allow only trusted origins, no wildcard with credentials
CORS replaces the need for authentication
Allow every origin so all of the sites can call the API freely
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: In one secure payment request, which step comes right after Authenticate (attach a signed token)?
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange. Serialize, Authenticate, Encrypt in transit, Validate, Verify integrity, Store safely.

questions.question: What is the last step of one secure request?
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: What is a JWT (JSON Web Token)?
options: An encrypted file that stores passwords so they can be read back later
A binary format for heavy internal service-to-service traffic
A browser rule that controls which websites may call the API
A signed token with a header, payload, and signature, used for stateless authentication
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: What is CORS?
options: A flow that grants limited access without passwords
A one-way fingerprint used to store passwords safely
A browser rule controlling which websites may call your API
A cap on the number of requests allowed per window
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.

questions.question: What is a digital signature?
options: Private key signs, public key verifies, giving non-repudiation
One shared key encrypts and decrypts the same message
A hash of the message plus a shared secret key
A list of roles with only the permissions needed
questions.explanation: Lesson 3 - Reliable and Secure Data Exchange.
